title: "our father"
hook: "Our Father" — the word he chose was the family one

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Jesus, the carpenter's son who ate with the wrong people on purpose. Did you pull out a chair for anyone? Today we start the prayer he taught. Day four.

If you know one prayer by heart, it's probably this one. Weddings, funerals, school assemblies, a locker room before a big game. Our Father, who art in heaven. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians all pray it, more than two billion people. For the next five days, we'll go through it one line at a time, from the first words to the last. Today, just the opening. Because the way you start talking to someone tells you who you think they are. And Jesus started with a family word.
screen: `THE PRAYER EVERYONE KNOWS.` → `FIVE DAYS, ONE LINE A DAY.` → `IT STARTS WITH A FAMILY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, as the King James Bible gives it in Matthew chapter six: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name." Start with father. The Gospels were written in Greek, and the word there is pater. But Jesus spoke Aramaic, and once, in Mark, the Gospel keeps his own word. In the garden, the night before he died, he prays: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee." Abba is the family word. What a child says at home, and what a grown son still says to his dad. You may have heard it means daddy. Most scholars say that goes too far: it isn't baby talk. But it isn't a courtroom title either. It's the word you'd use at the kitchen table. And Paul, writing to the Romans, says the first Christians prayed it too: "whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Now the other word. Our. Not my. The whole prayer never once says I, me or my. It's our, us, our, us, all the way through. Even said alone in a quiet room, the prayer assumes a family around you. Then hallowed: an old English word for holy. May your name be treated as holy. So the first line holds two things at once. Close enough to call him father. Still holy. That's line one of five.
screen: `PATER, ABBA — FATHER.` · `ABBA — THE KITCHEN-TABLE WORD.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `HALLOWED — HOLY.` · then, large: `CLOSE, AND STILL HOLY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of the word our, and let one person you love come to mind. On the second, widen it to the people you'll pass today, strangers included. On the third, if you pray, you can say the line: Our Father, which art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. If you don't, just rest in the word our. You're one of many, tonight.
Line one of the Lord's Prayer. Our Father: the family word, with a family around you. Fourth on your strand.
Your line to carry: you're not addressing a stranger. Today, when you talk to someone you love, use the name only you call them. Notice what that one word does. That's day four.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray the Lord's Prayer every day, and in most churches the congregation says it together, aloud, often standing.

fork.setup: you're teaching people to pray, and you choose the first word they'll say to God. which does Jesus choose?
fork.reveal: "our Father." and in Mark, when he prays himself, the Aramaic abba: the family word.

original.note: Greek, Matthew 6:9: our Father. behind it, many scholars hear the Aramaic abba.

trapdoor: what you thought: a formal way to open a prayer.
what it means: the family word — and our, not my.
what a scholar hears: Mark 14:36 and Romans 8:15 keep the Aramaic abba untranslated, a sign, many say, that the first Christians remembered Jesus praying that way.

notes: The hook uses the familiar spoken form 'who art in heaven'; the teach and practice quote the KJV 'which art'. Keeper may prefer one form throughout.
'Abba isn't baby talk' follows the scholarly correction of the older 'abba = daddy' claim (James Barr, 1988). Confirm wording.
'More than two billion' Christians is a round figure (about 2.4 billion is commonly cited).
